1.pericope_label: It is a good thing to give thanks unto the Lord, and to sing praises unto thy name, O most High... For thou, Lord, hast made me glad through thy work: I will triumph in the works of thy hands

schools.summary: Places the psalm liturgically and then corrects a famous misuse of it. It was the sabbath psalm of the post-exilic service, sung at the drink-offering of the first daily lamb, and the Talmud itself could not settle whether it looks back to the sabbath of creation or forward to the last sabbath of history. On the pairing of morning with lovingkindness and night with faithfulness, the assignment is judged a feature of Hebrew style, though a fitting one; and the gladness of the fourth verse, which in its Latin dress gave a famous poet an image of delight in natural beauty, is insisted to refer to works in history rather than in nature.

Denies that the day is holy in the sense of being devoted to idleness, since idleness could be no acceptable worship: it is holy in separating us from other occupations so that we may meditate on the divine works, our minds being inconstant and apt to wander when distracted. Right observance consists not in idleness, as some absurdly imagine, but in the celebration of the divine name. The goodness of thanksgiving is grounded on its being God's will, our reasonable service, and pleasant and profitable besides.

Refuses the title as evidence: it gives no information about time, occasion or author, the tradition that the first man spoke it is an idle conceit, and the psalm was more probably written by Levites near the close of the captivity. Notices how abruptly it opens. Reads the second verse as a plan for morning and evening prayer — mercy acknowledged for preservation through the night, faithfulness for the promise kept through the day — and, on the ten-stringed instrument, quotes a fourth-century allegory only to draw a historical inference from it about church practice.

Makes the sabbath a day not only of holy rest but of holy work, the rest in order to the work, its proper work being praise, which the other services must not thrust into a corner; calls praise the rent we pay our great Lord, so that we are unjust if we withhold it, and work that is its own wages. Divides the goodness of thanksgiving three ways — ethical, since it is the Lord's right; emotional, since it is pleasant; practical, since it draws others — and holds that a sabbath without thanksgiving is a sabbath profaned, since nature itself teaches the form in singing birds and warbling brooks.

Relocates the sabbath inward. Rest is from evil works, and a merely bodily observance abstains from good ones, since it is better to plough than to dance; the sabbath God proclaims is in the heart, for many are idle in their limbs while disturbed in conscience. It opens with the warning that no Christian should promise himself the happiness of the world, since God loves whether he caresses or threatens.

debates.question: Which sabbath does the psalm belong to?

positions.summary: The final sabbath of the world's history rather than the sabbath of creation, though the tradition itself was divided.
The age to come, which shall be all sabbath, of which believers already enjoy the beginning.
No particular sabbath: the title tells us nothing about time or occasion, and the psalm is likelier a late composition of the captivity.

debates.question: What is the work that made the psalmist glad?

positions.summary: Any or all of it — creation, providence, redemption, or the work of grace upon the soul.
God's wonders wrought in Israel's history, not the beauty of nature, despite the verse's long poetic afterlife.
Both revelations, the historical rule and the Creator's works, the ability to rejoice in either being itself a gift from above.

outliers.reading: Uses a fourth-century commentator's allegory of the ten-stringed instrument as evidence about church history rather than about the verse, arguing from the writer's silence that instrumental music was not then in use in Christian worship.

themes: It is a good thing to give thanks unto the Lord, and to sing praises unto thy name, O most High:
To shew forth thy lovingkindness in the morning, and thy faithfulness every night,
Upon an instrument of ten strings, and upon the psaltery; upon the harp with a solemn sound.
For thou, Lord, hast made me glad through thy work: I will triumph in the works of thy hands.

5.pericope_label: O Lord, how great are thy works! and thy thoughts are very deep... For, lo, thine enemies, O Lord, for, lo, thine enemies shall perish; all the workers of iniquity shall be scattered

schools.summary: Prefers plans or purposes to thoughts, and rejects the received construction of the seventh verse: the Authorised Version wrongly introduces a second conjunction, so that the line should read that in the springing of the wicked like grass all the workers of iniquity flourish to be destroyed for ever. A companion voice calls the prosperity of the ungodly a semblance lasting for a time, a historical occurrence repeated to the present day and to be closed by a decisive judgment, and reads the central verse as the moment when the oppressed church stands forth vindicated.

Spreads the works across nature, providence and grace, and reads the brutish man as one who, made far above the brute creatures, became by sinning like the beasts that perish, caring no more for an immortal soul than a beast that has none. Finds a deliberate antithesis in the central verse between the wicked and the Lord, and adds the hard corollary that God endures for ever to inflict the punishment, which is why the destruction is everlasting.

Calls the works multitudinous and splendid and the thoughts the designs from which they were formed, too profound to be fathomed. Insists that the two names for the unspiritual man are distinct: the first has mind but buried in flesh, the second has no mind at all and his stupidity is unavoidable. Draws the practical rule that God's favour is not measured by prosperity nor his disapproval by adversity, and keeps the balance of the central verse simple — the wicked brought down, the Lord exalted for his judgments as well as his mercies. A second voice glosses the deep thoughts as God's counsels in governing world and church.

Pairs act with plan — some men think but cannot work and others are drudges working without thought, whereas in the Eternal conception and execution go together — and finds man superficial where God is inscrutable. Marks the drop to the brutish man as a deliberate stoop, from the saint to the brute, and presses the flower figure on the wicked: they grow to die and blossom to be blasted. Supplies the proverb that the prosperity of fools shall slay them and that sheep designed for slaughter are put into the fattest pasture.

debates.question: Do the two names for the unspiritual man describe one failure or two?

positions.summary: Two, and sharply different: one has a mind buried in flesh, the other has none, and his stupidity is unavoidable.
Two, but along another line: in the first the moral sense never came into play, in the second it is overgrown by sensuality.
One type under two names — the man governed by sense rather than reason or faith.

debates.question: Is the received construction of the seventh verse sound?

positions.summary: No: the second conjunction is an insertion, and the line means that the flourishing of the wicked is itself unto their destruction.
Yes as it stands, and it describes a recurring historical pattern closed at last by a decisive judgment.

outliers.reading: Identifies the eighth verse as the numerical middle of the psalm and as the single fact the whole sabbath song exists to illustrate, making a structural observation the others do not attempt.

themes: O Lord, how great are thy works! and thy thoughts are very deep.
A brutish man knoweth not; neither doth a fool understand this.
When the wicked spring as the grass, and when all the workers of iniquity do flourish; it is that they shall be destroyed for ever:
But thou, Lord, art most high for evermore.
For, lo, thine enemies, O Lord, for, lo, thine enemies shall perish; all the workers of iniquity shall be scattered.

10.pericope_label: But my horn shalt thou exalt like the horn of an unicorn... To shew that the Lord is upright: he is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him

schools.summary: Identifies the horned animal with the oryx on ancient authority and reads the horn as defensive power and stately grace at once; a companion voice prefers buffalo, and recasts the following verse so that the eye looks upon insidious foes without fear and the ears listen without alarm. On the trees it notes that this is the only place where the palm serves as an emblem of moral rectitude, while the cedar had long been emblem of kingly might, and makes the temple itself the soil in which the righteous are planted or transplanted.

Applies the exalted horn to David's kingdom, to the Messiah as the horn of salvation raised in his house, and to every good man whom God exalts. Keeps to the mechanics of the figure — the palm rises against the greatest weight laid on it, its whole force in its top, which being cut off it dies — and notes that though the singular has led some to find Christ here, it is his people who are meant. Recalls that the temple had palm trees carved on its walls, and reads the planting as a bringing out of the world into Christ.

Overrules its own first suggestion of the oryx or buffalo in favour of the rhinoceros as the true single-horned creature of Scripture, and doubts any sacramental reference in the oil, thinking of ordinary anointings after bathing. Denies that the planting alludes to any actual trees near the tabernacle, reading it only as the righteous flourishing in God's ordinances as trees do in their proper soil. Turns antiquarian on the cedars, quoting a traveller's measurements, and closes soberly that it is a rare case to find a man in old age full of faith and spiritual activity. A second voice takes the anointing as the custom of joyful solemnities and the house as the church.

Leaves the horned animal unidentified, keeping only that it was the ancients' favourite symbol of unconquerable power, and objects that the translators' inserted phrase in the next verse should have been left out, since the psalmist leaves the space blank. Draws the palm from the desert — all its strength sent upward in one bold column, thriving in drought — and observes that grass, which makes hay for oxen, is emblem enough for the unregenerate, while cedars, which build the temple, are none too good for the heirs of heaven.

debates.question: What animal is the exalted horn taken from?

positions.summary: The oryx, one-horned on ancient authority.
The rhinoceros, which is the real single-horned creature of Scripture.
Unidentifiable — perhaps some gigantic ox now unknown; what matters is that it stood for unconquerable power.

debates.question: Should the translators' addition in the eleventh verse stand?

positions.summary: No: the psalmist deliberately leaves blank what he will see concerning his enemies, and no one has the right to fill it.
No, and the whole line should be recast: the eye looked on its foes without fear and the ear heard their rising without alarm.
The traditional supplement is right in substance: the enemies would be destroyed within the psalmist's own lifetime.

outliers.reading: Breaks off into natural history, reporting a traveller's measurements of the Lebanon cedars and their reputed age, and then denies outright that the psalm's planting alludes to any trees actually growing at the sanctuary.

themes: But my horn shalt thou exalt like the horn of an unicorn: I shall be anointed with fresh oil.
Mine eye also shall see my desire on mine enemies, and mine ears shall hear my desire of the wicked that rise up against me.
The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree: he shall grow like a cedar in Lebanon.
Those that be planted in the house of the Lord shall flourish in the courts of our God.
They shall still bring forth fruit in old age; they shall be fat and flourishing;
To shew that the Lord is upright: he is my rock, and there is no unrighteousness in him.
